e-10897.problem: Simplify the integral $\displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx$ using symmetry.
e-10897.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 2\int_{0}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx .
$$

Notice that $f(x) = x \sin{x}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =-x(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x) = x \sin{x}$ is an even function, we have

$$
\int_{-2}^2  x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx = 2 \int_{0}^2  x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx.
$$

e-10898.knowledge_point: Identifying Integrals That Evaluate to Zero
e-10898.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry?

- $\displaystyle \int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx$

- $\displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 (e^x+e^{-x}) \, \textrm dx$

- $\displaystyle \int_{-\pi}^{2\pi} \sin(2x) \, \textrm dx$
e-10898.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x) = f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x) = -f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
\int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x) = 4x^3$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =4(-x)^{3} \\  & =-4{x}^{3} \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
\int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx = 0.
$$

- The function $g(x) = e^x+e^{-x}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & ={e}^{(-x)}+{e}^{-(-x)} \\  & ={e}^{-x}+{e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}+{e}^{-x} \\  & \ne -g(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $h(x) = \sin(2x)$ is an odd function, but integral III is not of the form $\displaystyle \int_{-a}^a h(x)\,\textrm d x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. So, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

content.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Even Functions
content.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & =(-x)(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)={x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{4}\,{e}^{(-x)^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}} \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)={x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}{x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{5}{x}^{4}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=-2{x}^{4}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =-2(-x)^{4} \\  & =-2{x}^{4} \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=-2{x}^{4}$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}(-2{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{5}(-2{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x.
$$

content.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any even function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ is symmetric across the $y$-axis, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=-2{x}^{4}$ is an even function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =-2(-x)^{4} \\  & =-2{x}^{4} \\  & =f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=-2{x}^{4}$ is an even function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}(-2{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{0}^{5}(-2{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x.
$$
